privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: PureKit is built with a privacy-first approach. This policy explains how we handle your data — or more accurately, how we don't.

sections.heading: No Data Collection
sections.content: PureKit tools run in your browser using client-side JavaScript. Your text, files, images and any other input are processed on your device and are never sent to any server. We do not collect, store or have access to the data you process with our tools. The one exception is the website check described below, which needs the website address you enter.

sections.heading: Website Checks
sections.content: The PHP Version Checker and PHP2Shell Checker can check a website by its address. Browsers can't read another site's response headers, so when you use this feature, the address you enter is sent to a PureKit function running on Cloudflare. It requests that site's homepage (and, for WordPress sites, the public /wp-json/ address) and returns what the response headers show (such as X-Powered-By) and signs that the site runs PHP. We don't store the address or the result. Each check is counted in our Plausible analytics with only its outcome (version found, hidden, blocked or error), the PHP branch found (such as 8.3), the PHP2Shell verdict, whether the version came from the homepage or /wp-json/, and which tool was used. The address and anything else that identifies the checked site are never sent to analytics. Cloudflare's standard request logs apply, as described under Hosting & CDN.

sections.heading: Privacy-Friendly Analytics
sections.content: PureKit uses two privacy-respecting analytics services: Cloudflare Web Analytics and a self-hosted instance of Plausible Analytics. Neither uses cookies or tracks individual users. Cloudflare Web Analytics provides basic aggregate statistics (page views, referrers) without collecting personally identifiable information, and is GDPR and CCPA compliant. Plausible does not store IP addresses or raw User-Agent strings: they are combined with a salt that is rotated and deleted every 24 hours to count unique visitors per day, and are used to work out the browser, operating system, device type and approximate location (country, region, city). It does not track people across devices, websites or apps. We only see aggregate statistics such as page views, referrers, countries and counts of website checks by outcome.

sections.heading: No Cookies or Personal Tracking
sections.content: PureKit does not use cookies for tracking. We do not use Google Analytics, Facebook Pixel, or any similar invasive services. We don't use browser fingerprinting, device tracking, or any techniques to identify individual users.

sections.heading: No User Accounts
sections.content: PureKit does not require registration or user accounts. There is no login, no profile, and no personal information to provide.

sections.heading: Hosting & CDN
sections.content: PureKit is hosted on Cloudflare Pages: a static website plus the small function behind the website check. Cloudflare may collect standard server logs (IP address, user agent, timestamps) as part of their infrastructure. These logs are managed by Cloudflare under their own privacy policy and are not accessible to PureKit.

sections.heading: Third-Party Services
sections.content: PureKit does not integrate with any third-party services that process your data. Tool functionality runs in your browser, except the website check, which runs on Cloudflare as described above. No external APIs are called with your data.

sections.heading: Open Source
sections.content: PureKit's source code is publicly available. You can verify our privacy claims by inspecting the code yourself. There are no hidden network requests or data transmissions.

sections.heading: Changes to This Policy
sections.content: If we make changes to this privacy policy, we will update this page. Given our architecture (client-side processing, with the website check as the only server-side step), significant privacy changes are unlikely.

sections.heading: Contact
sections.content: If you have questions about this privacy policy, please contact us at support@purekit.dev.

faq.question: What is a UUID?
faq.answer: UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is a 128-bit identifier that is practically unique across all systems. UUID v4, which this tool generates, uses random numbers to create identifiers with an extremely low probability of collision. The format is: xxxxxxxx-xxxx-4xxx-yxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx.

faq.question: Is UUID the same as GUID?
faq.answer: Essentially yes. GUID (Globally Unique Identifier) is Microsoft's implementation of the UUID standard. They follow the same format and serve the same purpose. UUID is the more widely used term in non-Microsoft contexts.

faq.question: Are the generated UUIDs truly random?
faq.answer: Yes. This tool uses the Web Crypto API (crypto.randomUUID()), which provides cryptographically secure random values. The generated UUIDs are suitable for use as database primary keys, session tokens, and other security-sensitive identifiers.

understanding.title: Understanding JWT Structure
understanding.intro: JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) are a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims between two parties. Understanding their structure is essential for modern web authentication and authorization.

sections.heading: What is a JWT Token?
sections.content: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a self-contained token format used for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object. It consists of three parts separated by dots: Header.Payload.Signature. JWTs are commonly used for authentication and information exchange in modern web applications, APIs, and microservices architectures.

sections.heading: JWT Header
sections.content: The header typically consists of two parts: the token type (JWT) and the signing algorithm (e.g., HMAC SHA256 or RSA). The header is Base64Url encoded to form the first part of the JWT. Example: {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}. The algorithm field indicates how the token signature should be verified.

sections.heading: JWT Payload (Claims)
sections.content: The payload contains the claims - statements about an entity (typically the user) and additional data. There are three types of claims: registered claims (predefined like iss, exp, sub), public claims (custom but should be collision-resistant), and private claims (custom shared between parties). Common claims include exp (expiration time), iat (issued at), sub (subject/user ID), iss (issuer), and aud (audience).

sections.heading: JWT Signature
sections.content: The signature is created by encoding the header and payload with Base64Url, concatenating them with a dot, and then signing the result using the algorithm specified in the header with a secret key. The signature ensures that the token hasn't been tampered with. To verify a JWT, the receiver must have access to the same secret key (for HMAC) or public key (for RSA/ECDSA).

sections.heading: Bearer Tokens Explained
sections.content: Bearer tokens are a type of access token included in the HTTP Authorization header. The format is 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. JWTs are commonly used as bearer tokens in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows. When you paste a bearer token into our decoder, we automatically extract the JWT portion. Bearer tokens grant access to protected resources - anyone who possesses the token can use it, hence they must be kept secure and transmitted only over HTTPS.

sections.heading: Common JWT Use Cases
sections.content: Authentication: After login, the server issues a JWT that the client includes in subsequent requests. The server validates the token without querying the database. Authorization: JWTs can contain user roles and permissions in the payload. Information Exchange: JWTs securely transmit information between services because you can verify the sender and ensure data integrity. Single Sign-On (SSO): One token can authenticate a user across multiple applications. Stateless API Authentication: No need to maintain server-side session storage.

faq.question: What is a JWT token?
faq.answer: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token format used for securely transmitting information between parties. It consists of three Base64Url-encoded parts: header, payload, and signature, separated by dots. JWTs are commonly used for authentication and authorization in modern web applications.

faq.question: What is a bearer token?
faq.answer: A bearer token is an access token included in the Authorization HTTP header using the format 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. JWTs are frequently used as bearer tokens in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect protocols. Anyone who possesses a bearer token can use it to access protected resources, so they must be transmitted securely over HTTPS.

faq.question: Can I decode bearer tokens with this tool?
faq.answer: Yes! Our decoder automatically extracts the JWT from bearer token format. Simply paste the entire 'Bearer <token>' string or just the JWT portion. The decoder will handle both formats and display the decoded header, payload, and signature.

faq.question: Is JWT decoding safe? Will my token be uploaded?
faq.answer: Absolutely safe. All JWT decoding happens entirely in your browser using JavaScript - nothing is sent to any server. Your tokens never leave your device. We don't collect, store, or transmit any data. You can verify this by checking your browser's network tab or inspecting our open-source code.

faq.question: Can this tool verify JWT signatures?
faq.answer: Our tool decodes and displays the JWT structure but does not verify signatures because that would require access to your secret key. Signature verification should be done on your backend server where the secret key is stored securely. This tool is designed for inspection and debugging, not authentication.

faq.question: What are JWT claims?
faq.answer: JWT claims are statements about an entity (usually the user) contained in the payload. Common registered claims include: exp (expiration time), iat (issued at time), sub (subject/user identifier), iss (issuer), aud (audience), and nbf (not before). You can also include custom private claims specific to your application.

faq.question: JWT vs Session Authentication - what's the difference?
faq.answer: Session authentication stores user state on the server and uses a session ID in cookies. JWT authentication is stateless - all user information is encoded in the token itself. JWTs enable horizontal scaling and work well with microservices, but they cannot be easily revoked before expiration. Sessions require server-side storage but allow instant revocation.

faq.question: What is the difference between JWE and JWT?
faq.answer: JWT (JSON Web Token) is for signing data to ensure integrity and authenticity. JWE (JSON Web Encryption) is for encrypting data to ensure confidentiality. JWTs are typically signed (JWS - JSON Web Signature) but not encrypted, meaning anyone can decode and read the payload. JWE encrypts the entire payload so only parties with the decryption key can read it.

faq.question: Why does my JWT token show as expired?
faq.answer: JWTs include an 'exp' (expiration) claim that specifies when the token becomes invalid. Our decoder checks this timestamp against the current time and highlights expired tokens. Expired tokens should not be accepted by your API. Token expiration is a security feature to limit the window of potential misuse if a token is compromised.

understanding.title: Understanding Gemini Watermarks and How to Remove Them
understanding.intro: Google Gemini adds a semi-transparent watermark to AI-generated images. This guide explains what the Gemini watermark looks like, why it appears, and how our tool removes it using precise mathematical restoration — not destructive AI inpainting.

sections.heading: What Is the Gemini Watermark?
sections.content: The Gemini watermark is a semi-transparent logo overlay that Google applies to images generated by Gemini AI models (including Gemini 1.5, Gemini 2.0, and later versions). It typically appears as a small star-shaped icon or the Google Gemini logo in the corner of generated images. Users often describe it as the "Gemini star," "Gemini icon," or "Gemini mark." The watermark is embedded using alpha blending, meaning it modifies the actual pixel values of the image rather than being a separate layer.

sections.heading: Why Do Users Want to Remove the Gemini Watermark?
sections.content: There are several legitimate reasons to remove the Gemini watermark from images. Creators using AI-generated images for presentations, social media, or design work often need clean images without branding overlays. The watermark can be distracting in professional contexts, and users who have generated images for personal or commercial use may want a clean output. Additionally, photographers or designers who use Gemini for concept art or mood boards prefer to work with unmarked reference images.

sections.heading: How Does Gemini Watermark Removal Work?
sections.content: Unlike generic AI watermark removers that use inpainting (which guesses what pixels should look like), this tool uses reverse alpha blending — the exact mathematical inverse of how Google applied the watermark. The formula is: original_pixel = (watermarked_pixel - alpha * watermark_pixel) / (1 - alpha). Because we know the exact watermark pattern, position, and alpha values for each Gemini image size, the restoration is pixel-perfect. The multi-pass system fine-tunes the result and validates quality to ensure no artifacts remain.

sections.heading: Supported Gemini Image Sizes and Models
sections.content: This tool maintains a built-in catalog of all known Google Gemini output resolutions and watermark configurations. It supports images from Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0, and newer models across all standard aspect ratios (1:1, 4:3, 16:9, 3:4, 9:16). Resolution support ranges from 512px up to 4K. For non-standard crops or screenshots, the adaptive detection system scans the image to locate the watermark regardless of position.

sections.heading: Online Tool vs. Browser Extension
sections.content: Some users search for a Gemini watermark remover extension, but a browser-based web tool offers significant advantages. There is no installation or permissions required, it works on any device including mobile, and it receives instant updates when Google changes watermark patterns. Unlike extensions that may require broad browser permissions, this online tool processes everything locally in your browser tab with zero data transmission. Simply open the page, drop your image, and download the clean result.

sections.heading: Privacy and Security
sections.content: All watermark detection and removal processing happens entirely in your browser using JavaScript and the HTML5 Canvas API. Your images are never uploaded to any server, never stored, and never transmitted over the network. This makes the tool safe for sensitive or private AI-generated content. You can verify this by checking your browser's network tab — zero outbound requests are made during processing.

faq.question: How do I remove the Gemini watermark from an image?
faq.answer: Upload your Gemini AI-generated image to this tool — it automatically detects the watermark position and size, then applies reverse alpha blending to mathematically restore the original pixels. Click "Download Clean Image" to save the clean version. The entire process takes seconds and works in any browser.

faq.question: Is this Gemini watermark remover free?
faq.answer: Yes, completely free with no limits. There are no signups, no watermarks added to your output, no daily usage caps, and no premium tiers. The tool runs entirely in your browser, so there are no server costs to pass on to users.

faq.question: Can it remove the Gemini logo from images?
faq.answer: Yes. Whether you call it the Gemini watermark, Gemini logo, Gemini star, or Gemini icon, this tool detects and removes the same semi-transparent overlay that Google Gemini applies to AI-generated images. The removal works identically regardless of which term you use to describe it.

faq.question: How does the watermark removal work technically?
faq.answer: Google Gemini embeds its watermark using alpha blending: watermarked = original * (1 - alpha) + logo * alpha. This tool applies the exact inverse formula: original = (watermarked - alpha * logo) / (1 - alpha). Because we know the precise watermark pattern and alpha values, the restoration is mathematically exact — not a guess or AI-generated fill.

faq.question: Does it work with all Google Gemini models and image sizes?
faq.answer: Yes. The tool supports all known Gemini output resolutions from Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0, and newer models. It handles all standard aspect ratios and resolutions from 512px to 4K. An adaptive detection system also handles non-standard crops or screenshots where the image has been resized.

faq.question: Will removing the watermark affect image quality?
faq.answer: Pixels outside the watermark area are completely untouched. The watermark region is restored to near-original quality using mathematical reversal. The multi-pass system includes safety checks — if removal quality does not meet the threshold, the process is refined automatically. The result is visually indistinguishable from the original unwatermarked image.

faq.question: Do I need to install a browser extension?
faq.answer: No. This is a web-based tool that works directly in your browser. No extension, software download, or installation is needed. Just open the page and upload your image. The tool works on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices across all major browsers.

faq.question: Are my images uploaded to a server?
faq.answer: No. All processing happens 100% in your browser using JavaScript and the Canvas API. Your images never leave your device — nothing is uploaded, stored, or transmitted to any server. You can verify this by monitoring your browser's network tab during processing.

understanding.title: PHP Versions and Support Explained
understanding.intro: PHP releases one new minor version a year, usually in late November or early December. Each version moves through active support, security-only support and end of life. Knowing where your version stands tells you how urgently you need to upgrade.

sections.heading: How the PHP release cycle works
sections.content: According to php.net, each PHP branch is fully supported for two years after its first stable release, with reported bugs and security issues fixed in regular point releases. It then gets two more years of fixes for critical security issues only, released as needed. After those four years the branch reaches end of life and gets no more updates. Current branches stop receiving support on 31 December: PHP 8.4, for example, has active support until 31 Dec 2026 and security fixes until 31 Dec 2028.

sections.heading: Which PHP versions are supported right now
sections.content: As of October 2026, PHP 8.5 and 8.4 have active support, PHP 8.3 and 8.2 get security fixes only, and every version from 8.1 down has reached end of life. Security support for PHP 8.2 ends on 31 Dec 2026. The checker above calculates each status from today's date, so it stays correct as these dates pass.

sections.heading: How to check your PHP version
sections.content: Enter a site's address on the Website tab to see the version it reports in its X-Powered-By header. On the server itself, run php -v, but note that the command line can use a different PHP binary than your website. To see what the web server runs, upload a file containing <?php echo PHP_VERSION; or phpinfo(); open it in a browser, then delete it. In WordPress, go to Tools → Site Health → Info and open the Server section.

sections.heading: Why a website might hide its PHP version
sections.content: The X-Powered-By header is controlled by the expose_php setting in php.ini. Many hosts turn it off, and proxies or CDNs often remove it, so a missing header doesn't mean a site isn't running PHP. Hiding the version doesn't make an outdated PHP any safer; only upgrading does.

sections.heading: How the code compatibility check works
sections.content: The checker removes comments and strings, then looks for the syntax, functions and classes listed in the official php.net migration guides for every release from PHP 5.6 to 8.5. The highest version it finds is the minimum your code needs. Removed functions set an upper limit, and deprecated features show which versions will print deprecation notices. It's pattern matching rather than a full parser: it doesn't run your code, follow includes, or check extensions and Composer dependencies. Treat the result as a strong hint and confirm it with your tests or a tool like PHPCompatibility for PHP_CodeSniffer.

sections.heading: Polyfills and the minimum version
sections.content: Built-in functions such as str_contains() or array_find() can be added to older PHP versions with a polyfill, for example the symfony/polyfill packages or the compat.php file that WordPress ships. Syntax such as enums, match expressions or readonly properties can't be polyfilled. That's why the checker shows the version needed for the syntax alone next to the overall minimum, and marks functions and classes as polyfillable.

faq.question: How do I check my PHP version?
faq.answer: For a website, enter its address on the Website tab. On the server, run php -v, or create a PHP file containing <?php echo PHP_VERSION; and open it in your browser to see the version your web server uses. In WordPress, go to Tools → Site Health → Info → Server. Paste what you find on the Version tab to see whether that version is still supported.

faq.question: What is the latest PHP version?
faq.answer: PHP 8.5 is the newest branch. It was released on 20 November 2025, and as of October 2026 its latest patch release is 8.5.12. A new minor version usually comes out each year in late November or early December.

faq.question: Is PHP 7.4 still supported?
faq.answer: No. PHP 7.4 reached end of life on 28 November 2022 and no longer gets security fixes from the PHP project. Some Linux distributions and hosts maintain their own patched packages, but php.net strongly urges users of unsupported versions to upgrade to a current one.

faq.question: Which PHP versions are still supported?
faq.answer: As of October 2026, PHP 8.5 and 8.4 have active support, while PHP 8.3 and 8.2 get security fixes only (8.2 until 31 Dec 2026, 8.3 until 31 Dec 2027). PHP 8.1 and older are end of life. The table above lists every branch and works out each status from today's date.

faq.question: Is my PHP version affected by PHP2Shell?
faq.answer: On PHP 8.2 to 8.5, every release below 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 is affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), and each result above says whether yours is. PHP 8.1 and older get no fixed release. The PHP2Shell Checker explains who is at risk and what to do.

faq.question: How do I find the minimum PHP version my code needs?
faq.answer: Open the Check code compatibility tab and paste your code. The checker lists every feature that needs a specific PHP version, such as enums (8.1) or the nullsafe operator (8.0), and reports the highest one as the minimum. It also flags removed functions like mysql_query() or each() that stop code from running on newer versions.

faq.question: Can this tool check a website's PHP version from its URL?
faq.answer: Yes. Enter the address on the Website tab. Browsers can't read another site's response headers, so PureKit's server requests the site's homepage (for WordPress sites that hide it there, also the public /wp-json/ address) and reads its X-Powered-By header. Many sites hide the version; in that case the checker shows signs that the site runs PHP, such as a PHPSESSID cookie or WordPress, and you'll need to check on the server.

faq.question: Why does my server show an older patch number than the latest release?
faq.answer: Linux distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian and Red Hat often backport security fixes into their own PHP packages without changing the upstream version number. A version like 8.1.2-1ubuntu2.14 can include fixes released long after 8.1.2. Check your distribution's security notices to see what is patched.

faq.question: Is my code uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: No. Code analysis and version lookups run in your browser, and nothing you paste is sent anywhere. Only the Website tab uses PureKit's server: it receives the address you enter, requests that site's homepage (plus /wp-json/ for WordPress sites), and returns what the headers show. The address isn't stored; our analytics only count each check by outcome, such as version found or hidden.

understanding.title: PHP2Shell Explained
understanding.intro: PHP2Shell is the name given to two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which the PHP project fixed on 21 October 2026. Both can let an attacker run code on a server without logging in, and both are rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0.

sections.heading: What the two vulnerabilities are
sections.content: CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption: if PHP runs out of memory while internal request data is only partly initialized, request cleanup can treat that invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state: state that belongs to one request can survive after its memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker can use it before normal initialization resets it. According to BleepingComputer, researchers from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz found the flaws.

sections.heading: Who is at risk
sections.content: The PHP advisory says all PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It rates the risk highest for mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit lets an unauthenticated request trigger the attack before any application code runs. So the CMS or framework you use doesn't matter; the PHP version your server runs does.

sections.heading: Affected and fixed versions
sections.content: The GitHub advisories list every release below PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 as affected, and those four releases contain the fixes. PHP 8.6.0 RC4 includes them too. PHP 8.1 and older get no new releases. Given the severity, the PHP team published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 for people who build PHP themselves, and some Linux distributions and LTS vendors provide backported packages.

sections.heading: How to fix it
sections.content: Update to a fixed release. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so updated packages may already be available from your vendor. On shared hosting, switch to a fixed version in your control panel or ask your host whether they've installed the update. Restart PHP-FPM, Apache or your PHP workers afterwards so the new version is the one serving requests. If you're on PHP 8.1 or older, plan the move to a supported version; PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on 31 December 2026.

sections.heading: If you can't update right away
sections.content: The advisory lists interim measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths but don't make an installation safe. For CVE-2026-109618: set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can't override (such as php_admin_value), use container or cgroup memory limits as the availability boundary, keep post_max_size low (8M without file uploads, 32M with them) with upload_max_filesize below it, and enforce request size and count limits at the web server or proxy. For CVE-2026-109619: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool (not with ini_set() or .user.ini) and restart every worker; on PHP 8.5, also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Read the full list in the official advisory before changing production settings.

sections.heading: Is PHP2Shell being exploited?
sections.content: The PHP team describes a demonstrated exploit against mod_php. BleepingComputer reported that Cloudflare's CTO saw early attacks targeting both vulnerabilities before the patches were released, and that the UK's National Cyber Security Centre urged organizations to update immediately or take affected systems offline. Reports differ on how widely the flaws are being exploited, so treat any unpatched server as at risk.

sections.heading: What this checker can and can't tell you
sections.content: It compares a PHP version with the fixed releases. It doesn't test for the vulnerability or send exploit traffic, and it can't see whether your vendor backported the fix or whether interim mitigations are in place. Many websites hide their PHP version; a hidden version means you need to check on the server, not that you're safe.

faq.question: What is PHP2Shell?
faq.answer: PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, fixed on 21 October 2026. They can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on servers that use PHP to serve web requests. Both are rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0.

faq.question: Which PHP versions fix PHP2Shell?
faq.answer: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, released on 21 October 2026, fix both vulnerabilities. For the PHP 8.6 pre-release, 8.6.0 RC4 includes the fixes. Any earlier release in these branches is affected.

faq.question: Is PHP 7.4 or 8.1 affected?
faq.answer: The PHP project no longer releases PHP 8.1 or older, so there's no fixed 7.4 or 8.1 version. Because of the severity, the PHP team published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, and some Linux distributions and LTS vendors ship backported packages. Unless your vendor confirms a backport, treat these versions as vulnerable and upgrade.

faq.question: How do I check if my website is affected?
faq.answer: Enter your site's address in the checker above. If the site shows its PHP version, you'll see straight away whether it's affected. If the version is hidden, run php -v on the server, check your hosting control panel, or in WordPress go to Tools → Site Health → Info → Server, then enter the version here.

faq.question: Does hiding the PHP version protect me?
faq.answer: No. Turning off expose_php or removing the X-Powered-By header only hides the version from outside checks like this one. The vulnerabilities are in PHP itself, so an unpatched server stays vulnerable.

faq.question: Is WordPress affected by PHP2Shell?
faq.answer: WordPress isn't the vulnerable part; PHP is. Any WordPress site whose server runs an affected PHP version is at risk, whatever the WordPress version. Check your PHP version under Tools → Site Health → Info → Server, and ask your host to update PHP if it's affected.

faq.question: I'm on shared hosting. What should I do?
faq.answer: Check which PHP versions your hosting control panel offers and switch to a fixed release if one is available. If not, contact your host and ask whether they've installed the PHP2Shell fixes.

faq.question: Does this checker attack or scan my site?
faq.answer: No. It makes at most two ordinary requests, like a browser would: the homepage, plus the public /wp-json/ address for WordPress sites that hide the version on the homepage. It reads the response headers, doesn't send exploit traffic, and doesn't store the address.
